Here is a structured 12-week muscle-building plan for a 26-year-old vegan client with access to a full gym. The plan targets ~150 g protein per day from plant sources, includes training phases, weekly progression, exercise selections, sets/reps, and nutrition/recovery notes. It assumes a recreational lifter with general training history; adjust loads based on technique and rate of perceived exertion.

Overview
- Goal: Lean muscle gain (hypertrophy) with gradual progression
- Duration: 12 weeks
- Training frequency: 4 days per week (Upper/Lower split), with optional 5th and 6th cardio/recovery days as active recovery
- Weekly structure: 4 main resistance training days + optional lighter cardio or mobility work on rest days
- Progressive plan: Linear progression in sets/reps/load within mesocycles, with a deload at Week 11–12 if needed
- Nutrition: Target 150 g protein/day from plant sources; total calories tailored to support muscle gain without excessive fat gain. Hydration and micronutrient focus included
- Recovery: Sleep target 7–9 hours, stretching, mobility, and periodization to manage fatigue

Assumptions and constraints
- Equipment: Full gym (barbells, dumbbells, machines, cables)
- Vegan protein sources: pea, soy, rice, hemp, lentils, beans, quinoa, chia/flax,Seitan (gluten), nutritionally complete blends, etc.
- No eggs, dairy, meat, fish, or other animal products
- Protein timing: distribute protein evenly across 4–5 daily servings
- Fiber and caloric distribution: moderate carbs pre/post-workout; fats kept moderate

Phase 1: Foundation and hypertrophy acclimation (Weeks 1–4)
Goals:
- Mastering form, build exercise literacy, establish consistent protein intake
- Introduce progressive overload basics, accumulate training volume

Weekly structure (4 days: Upper A, Lower A, Upper B, Lower B)
- Reps: 8–12 for hypertrophy, RPE 7–8

Nutrition notes Week 1–4

Phase 2: Progressive overload and symmetry (Weeks 5–8)
Goals:
- Increase training volume moderately and introduce more compound loading
- Emphasize muscular balance with upper/lower pairs; begin peaking some lifts

Weekly structure remains 4 days, with minor adjustments
 Week 5

- Deload or transition to active recovery:
  - Light technique work and mobility
  - 2–3 sets of each movement at 50–60% effort for form

- Protein: maintain ~150 g/day
- Energy: align with aim of ~0–300 kcal/day surplus depending on weight changes
- Hydration and supplement plan continues

Programming details and progression rules
- Progressive overload: aim to increase load by small increments (2.5–5 kg on major lifts) once you can complete top end of target reps with good form for all sets in a given week
- Reps and sets: Weeks 1–4 use 8–12 reps; Weeks 5–8 use 6–12 with heavier emphasis on lower reps for main compounds; Weeks 9–12 use 4–6 reps for main lifts with higher weights, keeping accessory work in 8–12 range
- Exercise substitutions: If needed due to equipment or injury, substitute with safe alternatives maintaining movement pattern (e.g., replace back squat with goblet squat, barbell row with one-arm dumbbell row)
- Technique: prioritize form; elbows tucked, neutral spine, controlled reps; use spotter for heavy bench and squats if needed

Recovery and lifestyle
- Sleep: 7–9 hours per night
- Daytime activity: light movement on off days (walking, mobility work)
- Mobility: include 10–15 minutes post-workout and on rest days for hips, shoulders, wrists, and thoracic spine

- B12, D, iodine, iron, zinc, calcium: ensure fortified foods or supplements as needed; consider an iron and zinc check if fatigue or symptoms present
- Omega-3s: include ALA sources (chia, flax, walnuts); consider algal DHA/EPA supplement if needed

Here are practical, evidence-informed options for choosing a plant-based protein powder for a vegan client aiming ~150 g protein per day. I’ll outline top protein types, what to look for on labels, practical pros/cons, and a few product suggestions at different price points. Key protein options (plant-based)
- Pea protein: high in leucine among plant proteins, good amino acid profile, easily digestible. Often low in fat and carbs.
- Soy protein: complete protein with a strong essential amino acid profile, similar digestion to dairy proteins for many people; some avoid due to phytoestrogens concerns (generally safe in typical intakes).
- Rice protein: good in combination with other plant proteins to balance amino acids; often low in lysine, so pair with legumes.
- Hemp protein: decent protein content with healthy fats and fiber; not as high in protein per scoop and has a stronger earthy taste; good for variety.
- Blends (e.g., pea+rice, pea+soy, hemp+rice): designed to provide a complete amino acid profile and better texture/flavor.

What to look for on the label
- Protein per serving: aim for 20–30 g of protein per scoop, depending on your client’s daily plan to hit 150 g total across 4–6 servings.
- Amino acid profile: check leucine content (rough proxy for anabolic stimulus). A target of around 2.5–3 g leucine per day from protein sources helps with MPS when spread across meals; roughly 1–2 g leucine per 20–25 g protein per meal is common guidance.
- Complete protein: ideally powders that provide all essential amino acids (pea+rice blends, soy isolate, or soy+others).
- Digestibility and added enzymes: look for vegan-friendly enzymes or digestive aids if GI distress is an issue.
- Carbohydrates and fats: check if the powder includes extra sweeteners, sugar alcohols, or fats; many athletes prefer low-sugar options.
- Additives: minimal artificial flavors, colors, and preservatives. Avoid powders with heavy fillers.
- Allergen considerations: if she has soy or gluten sensitivities, check for cross-contamination and choose certified gluten-free or soy-free options as needed.
- Sustainability and ethics: for vegan clients who care about sourcing, consider certifications (organic, non-GMO, verified vegan) and transparent ingredient sourcing.

Practical recommendations by scenario
- Best overall for most vegan athletes: a high-quality pea protein isolate or a pea-protein blend (pea+rice). Advantages: clean taste, good digestibility, complete essential amino acids when blended; often available in unflavored or vanilla.
- If aiming for the most complete amino acid profile without blends: a soy protein isolate (if tolerated and not avoided for personal reasons).
- For variety and texture: a blend of pea protein and rice or a hemp+pea blend to vary amino acid profile and mouthfeel; can be smoother or grittier depending on formulation.
- For those needing higher protein per scoop: look for 25–30 g per scoop from a blend; sometimes blends use multiple proteins to achieve higher protein density per scoop.
- Flavor and mixability: choose flavors you know your client will enjoy; unflavored mixes provide flexibility for savory applications, smoothies, and breakfast recipes.

Sample product categories (not endorsements)
- Isolate/Concentrate blends: pea isolate, soy isolate, or pea+rice blends
- Blends with added amino acids: some blends include BCAA profile optimization or extra leucine
- Hydration/energy variants: some powders include added electrolytes or carbs; consider depending on her post-workout nutrition plan

Implementation tips
- Hitting 150 g/day: if you target roughly 4–5 protein servings per day, a 25–30 g protein powder per serving can help you reach the total efficiently. For example: 6 meals with 25 g each equals 150 g; or 5 meals with 30 g each and a smaller snack will also work.
- Timing: post-workout protein within 60–90 minutes supports recovery; incorporate protein powder as a shake or smoothie in that window, then rely on whole-food protein sources for other meals.
- GI considerations: some clients experience bloating with certain proteins. Start with 20–25 g per serving and assess tolerance, then adjust type or amount.
- Allergen and cross-contamination checks: if she has additional intolerances (gluten, soy), choose product lines that are certified gluten-free or soy-free as needed.

Sample starter options (generic, widely available)
- Option A: Pea protein isolate powder (unflavored or vanilla) + blend with unsweetened fortified plant milk

Here is a complete, integrated 12-week muscle-building plan for your vegan client. It combines the 4-day Upper/Lower resistance template, Phase-specific progression, the added cardio plan, a structured cheat meal day option, and the breakfast/post-workout and protein-powder guidance already discussed. It’s written to be ready-to-deliver as a week-by-week program. If you want, I can tailor exact loads to her current 1RM estimates; for now I’ve included load progressions in a conservative, scalable format so you can plug in real numbers.

Assumptions
- Equipment: Full gym (barbells, dumbbells, machines, cables)
- Training days: 4 days/week (Upper A, Lower A, Upper B, Lower B)
- Cardio: 2–3 sessions/week as described (Phase-based)
- Nutrition: vegan diet targeting ~150 g protein/day, adequate calories for lean mass gain
- Cheat meal day: 1 per week (optional), scheduled as noted
- Rest: 7–9 hours sleep recommended; mobility and recovery included

Weekly structure overview
- Weeks 1–4: Phase 1 – Foundation and hypertrophy acclimation
- Weeks 5–8: Phase 2 – Progressive overload and symmetry
- Weeks 9–12: Phase 3 – Intensification with pushed intensity on main lifts
- Cardio: Phase-appropriate; included on rest days or post-workout when energy allows

Phase 1: Foundation and hypertrophy acclimation (Weeks 1–4)
Goals
- Master technique, establish baseline volume, begin progressive overload
- Hit ~150 g/day protein; build habit of even protein distribution
- Introduce cardio for base conditioning and recovery

Weekly schedule (4 days resistance; 2 cardio options built-in)
- Week 1–4 pattern: Upper A, Lower A, Upper B, Lower B

Week 1
- Day 1 Upper A
  - Bench Press or Incline Dumbbell Press: 3×8–10
  - Barbell Row or Pendlay Row: 3×8–10
  - Overhead Press: 3×8–10
  - Dumbbell Lateral Raise: 3×12
  - Dumbbell Curl: 3×10–12
  - Tricep Pushdown: 3×10–12
- Day 2 Lower A
  - Back Squat: 3×8–10
  - Romanian Deadlift: 3×8–10
  - Leg Press or Walking Lunges: 3×10–12
  - Leg Curls: 3×10–12
  - Calf Raises: 4×12–15
- Day 3 Upper B
  - Push-ups or Chest-supported Machine Press: 3×8–12
  - Lat Pulldown or assisted Pull-ups: 3×8–12
  - Dumbbell Shoulder Press: 3×8–12
  - Chest Fly (cable/dumbbell): 3×10–12
  - Hammer Curls: 3×10–12
  - Tricep Dips or Skull Crushers: 3×10–12
- Day 4 Lower B
  - Deadlift (conventional or sumo, lighter): 3×6–8
  - Front Squat or Goblet Squat: 3×8–10
  - Leg Extensions: 3×12
  - Hamstring Curls: 3×12
  - Calf Raises: 4×12–15
- Cardio
  - Phase 1: 2 sessions/week
    - A: 20–25 min steady-state at 60–70% HRmax (walk/cycle)
    - B: 15–20 min low-intensity + mobility (optional)
- Cheat meal day: Optional 1 per week on a rest or lighter-day if desired (see cheat meal section for structure)
- Nutrition notes: 150 g/day protein distributed across 4–5 meals. Maintain maintenance calories + 250–350 kcal surplus; hit fiber targets with whole plant foods
- Recovery: 7–9 hours sleep; 10–15 min mobility daily; track progress and fatigue

Weeks 2–4: progression within Phase 1
- Week 2: maintain structure; aim to increase load slightly on at least 1–2 main lifts if technique is solid; keep RPE around 7–8
- Week 3: add 1–2 accessory sets to key lifts or increase one rep in main sets (progressive overload)
- Week 4: deload week behavior or light technique week
  - Option: reduce volume to 60–70% of Week 3 for technique and recovery
- Cardio (Phase 1): keep to 2 sessions; you may swap one session to 15–20 min mobility + light cardio
- Cheat meal day: optional; if used, ensure protein targets stay on track and calories balanced across the week

Phase 2: Progressive overload and symmetry (Weeks 5–8)
Goals
- Increase training volume moderately
- Begin heavier loading on main lifts; maintain good technique
- Sustain ~150 g/day protein and ensure caloric balance

Weekly schedule (4 days)
- Week 5
  - Day 1 Upper A
    - Bench Press: 4×6–8
    - Barbell Row: 4×6–8
    - Overhead Press: 3×6–8
    - Lateral Raises: 3×12–15
    - Cable Tricep Pushdown: 3×10–12
    - Dumbbell Curl: 3×10–12
  - Day 2 Lower A
    - Back Squat: 4×6–8
    - Romanian Deadlift: 3×8
    - Leg Press: 3×10–12
    - Leg Curl: 3×10–12
    - Calf Raises: 4×12–15
  - Day 3 Upper B
    - Incline Dumbbell Press: 4×6–8
    - Pull-Ups/Lat Pulldown: 4×6–8
    - Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press: 3×8–10
    - Chest Fly (cable): 3×10–12
    - Cable Hammer Curl: 3×10–12
    - Skull Crushers or Overhead Tricep Extension: 3×10–12
  - Day 4 Lower B
    - Deadlift: 4×5–6
    - Front Squat or Goblet Squat: 3×8
    - Romanian Deadlift (light/moderate): 3×8
    - Leg Extension: 3×12
    - Hamstring Curl: 3×12
    - Calf Raises: 4×12–15
  - Cardio: 2 sessions; maintain steady-state or intervals as described below
- Weeks 6–7
  - Similar structure to Week 5, add 1–2 more sets for main lifts or increase load modestly (maintain RPE 8–9 on top sets)
  - Rest intervals: 75–90 seconds on accessory, 2–3 minutes on main lifts
- Week 8
  - Deload week or reduced volume
  - Upper A: 2–3 sets per main lift at 60–70% 1RM
  - Lower A: 2–3 sets per main lift at 60–70% 1RM
  - Upper B: 2–3 sets per main lift at 60–70% 1RM
  - Lower B: 2–3 sets per main lift at 60–70% 1RM
  - Cardio: optional light (20–25 minutes) with mobility
- Nutrition Weeks 5–8
  - Protein target maintained ~150 g/day
  - Calorie plan: adjust to slow/steady gains; if gains are slow, add 100–200 kcal/day; if gains are excessive, pull back 100–200 kcal
  - Hydration and micronutrients: continue supplementation as needed
- Cheat meal
  - If used, schedule 1 cheat every week or every 10–14 days depending on adherence
  - Ensure protein targets stay consistent; the cheat meal primarily contributes to surplus calories

Phase 3: Intensification and conditioning refinement (Weeks 9–12)
Goals
- Maximize hypertrophy with higher intensity on main lifts
- Maintain technique with longer rest, but manage fatigue
- Preserve symmetry and core strength

Week 9
- Day 1 Upper A
  - Bench Press: 5×5 (aim for RPE 8–9)
  - Barbell Row: 5×5
  - Overhead Press: 4×6
  - Lateral Raises: 3×12–15
  - Tricep Pushdown: 3×8–10
  - Curl: 3×8–10
- Day 2 Lower A
  - Back Squat: 5×5
  - Romanian Deadlift: 4×6
  - Leg Press: 3×8–10
  - Leg Curl: 3×8–10
  - Calf Raises: 4×12–15
- Day 3 Upper B
  - Incline Press: 5×5
  - Pull-Ups/Lat Pulldown: 4×6–8
